known_from: ch02-term-registry.json (terms defined there count as known in every chapter)

terms.definition: the observation that the combined answer of many people is often better than one expert's answer.
a model that predicts a class (a category) rather than a number.

one of the categories a classifier chooses between; in the moons data, class 0 or class 1. Careful: Python also says "class" for a blueprint objects are made from (each Scikit-Learn model type, such as `VotingClassifier`, is one); the sentence always shows which.
turning the members' answers into one answer, e.g. by majority vote or by averaging.
a 2006–2009 public competition to predict film ratings; the winning teams combined many models.
each member names one class; the class with the most votes wins.
each member gives a probability for each class; the probabilities are averaged, and the class with the highest average wins.
the answer given by more than half of the voters (or, with several choices, by the most voters).
a model for classification (despite its name) that outputs a probability for each class; the book's Chapter 4 covers it.
support vector machine (chapter 5): a model that separates the classes with the widest possible street; `SVC` is Scikit-Learn's SVM classifier.
a model only slightly better than random guessing, e.g. right 51% of the time on a yes/no question.
a model that reaches high accuracy.
a number from 0 to 1 (0% to 100%) for how likely something is.
the rule that the average over many independent tries settles close to the true rate: toss a 51% coin enough times and the share of heads settles near 51%.
said of two sources whose mistakes are unrelated: one being wrong tells you nothing about whether the other is wrong.
mistakes that come together: when one member is wrong on a row, the others tend to be wrong on that same row.
how differently the members of an ensemble make their mistakes; the more different, the more the vote helps.
the share of rows a classifier gets right: 0.912 means 91.2 rows out of 100.
a made-up two-feature dataset from Scikit-Learn's `make_moons()`: two interlocking crescent shapes, one per class, with some random scatter (noise).
the Scikit-Learn class that wraps several classifiers into one voting ensemble.
the Scikit-Learn function that cuts the rows at random into a training part and a test part (75% and 25% by default).
a fresh, untrained copy of a model with the same settings.
said of probabilities that can be taken at face value: among rows given 80%, about 80% really are that class.

exclude: Ensembles: Gradient boosting, random forests, bagging, voting, stacking
terms.definition: bootstrap aggregating: train the same algorithm many times, each copy on its own random sample of the rows drawn WITH replacement, then combine their answers.
the same as bagging, but the sample for each copy is drawn WITHOUT replacement (no row twice in one sample).
drawing rows so that each drawn row goes back into the pool and can be drawn again; "without replacement" means it cannot.
a random sample of rows drawn with replacement; in Scikit-Learn, `bootstrap=True` switches this on.
error that comes from the model being too simple for the problem, so it is wrong in the same way whatever sample it trained on.

how much a model's answers would swing if you trained it again on a different sample of the same data. (Chapter 2's variance is a number for how spread out one column's values are; here the word describes a model.)
one of the processors inside a computer's CPU; separate cores can run separate work at the same time.
run at the same time, on different cores or machines.
the line where the model's answer changes from one class to the other.
the setting for how many member models an ensemble trains.
the setting for how many rows each member draws for training.
how many CPU cores to use; -1 means all of them.
the value that occurs most often in a list.
scoring each training row with only the members that never drew it, which gives an accuracy estimate without a separate validation set.
an estimate that comes out lower (worse) than the real result.
a prediction for a row made by a model that was trained without that row.
bagging that samples both rows and features for each member.
bagging that keeps every row but samples the features for each member.
how many features each split (or each member) may look at.
whether features are sampled with replacement (the column version of `bootstrap`).
having very many columns, e.g. one per pixel of an image.
one yes/no question inside a decision tree, such as "is x1 at most 0.35?", which divides the rows at a node into two groups.
one box of a decision tree: it either asks a yes/no question or, at the bottom, gives the answer.
a node at the bottom of a tree: it holds the answer for every row that reaches it.
the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the original: √100 = 10, √2 ≈ 1.41.
Scikit-Learn's random forest for classification.
a tree setting: each tree may have at most this many leaves.
the number a tree's split compares a feature against, e.g. the 0.35 in "x1 at most 0.35".
extremely randomized trees: a random forest whose trees pick each split's threshold at random instead of searching for the best one.
how mixed the classes are among the rows at a node: 0 when they are all one class ("pure").
a dataset of 70,000 small (28 × 28 pixel) images of handwritten digits, from the book's Chapter 3.
training members one after another, each one focused on what the ones before it still get wrong.
adaptive boosting: after each member, raise the weight of the rows it got wrong, so the next member pays more attention to them.
a number per training row saying how much that row counts during training; in AdaBoost all rows start equal.
a decision tree with a single question (max_depth=1).
a number that scales how big each correction is: smaller means more cautious steps.
log(x) answers "e to what power gives x?" (e ≈ 2.718); log(1) = 0, log of a number above 1 is positive, below 1 negative.
exp(x) = e to the power x (e ≈ 2.718); always positive. exp(−1) ≈ 0.37, exp(0) = 1, exp(0.754) ≈ 2.125.
divide every weight by their total, so they add up to 1 again.
"the choice that makes this biggest": argmax over k returns the class k with the biggest total, not the total itself.
the multi-class version of AdaBoost that Scikit-Learn runs; with two classes it is the same as the equations shown.

exclude: Ensembles: Gradient boosting, random forests, bagging, voting, stacking
terms.definition: boosting where each new tree is trained on the leftover errors (residuals) of all the trees before it, and the predictions are added up. GBRT = gradient boosted regression trees.
what is left over: the true value minus the prediction so far. Truth 3.0, prediction 2.6: residual 0.4.
using a small learning rate so each tree's contribution is shrunk; it needs more trees but usually generalizes better.
to work well on new rows the model has never seen, not only on its training rows.
stop adding trees (or training rounds) as soon as the score on held-out rows stops improving.
gradient boosting where each tree trains on a random fraction of the rows (the `subsample` setting).
HGB: gradient boosting that first puts every feature's values into at most 255 buckets (bins), which makes training much faster on big tables.
replacing each value with the number of the bucket (bin) it falls into, e.g. every income between 3.10 and 3.15 becomes bucket 87.
a Scikit-Learn transformer that replaces each text category with a whole number: <1H OCEAN → 0, INLAND → 1, and so on.
a Scikit-Learn tool that applies a transformation to chosen columns only; `remainder="passthrough"` passes the other columns through unchanged.
the HGB setting that says which columns hold categories (not quantities).

exclude: Ensembles: Gradient boosting, random forests, bagging, voting, stacking
terms.definition: stacked generalization: instead of voting, train a final model (the blender) to combine the members' predictions.
the final model in stacking: its inputs are the other models' predictions, and it learns how to combine them.
a Scikit-Learn function that gives a prediction for every training row from a copy of the model trained without that row (cross-validation).
the StackingClassifier setting that chooses the blender.
of a classifier's "yes" answers, the share that are correct (the book's Chapter 3).
a column is high-cardinality when it has many distinct values (a price column has thousands; a yes/no column has two).
the one number training tries to make small: how wrong the predictions are overall. For a regression tree here it is the squared error.
a way to train a model: repeatedly take a small step in the direction that makes the loss smaller fastest (the book's chapter 4).
